entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To flatter someone with power, such as a boss, teacher or coach, or do favors for them, to win their approval.
entries.usage: Always critical: you say it about other people, or about yourself only as a joke. Common in casual talk about work and school, often in the progressive (*He's always sucking up to the boss*); a person who does this is *a suck-up*. Too casual and a little rude for formal writing, where *flatter* or *curry favor with* fit.
examples: Ever since the promotion was announced, Dave's been **sucking up to** the boss in every meeting.
My little brother **sucks up to** Grandma so she'll slip him some extra cash.
I'm not going to **suck up to** my professor just to get a better grade.

drill.sentence: She brings the coach coffee every morning and laughs at all his jokes; she's totally {{sucking up}} to him.
drill.hint: flattering him to get on his good side (not *kissing up* or *cozying up*)

entries.related: *kiss up to someone* — same meaning, a little softer; *brown-nose* — same, cruder; *butter someone up* — flatter someone before asking for something.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To accept something about yourself, or something you did, fully and confidently, without hiding it, apologizing for it or making excuses.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech, coaching and self-help talk, often as encouragement: *It's your style, so own it.* It covers both proudly accepting something different about yourself and taking full responsibility for a mistake (*own your mistakes*). Fine in spoken feedback at work, but it sounds like a pep talk in formal writing.
examples: You missed the deadline, so just **own it** and tell the client what happened.
Gray hair at thirty-five? I've decided to **own it**.
If you're going to wear a bright orange suit to the wedding, you have to **own it**.

drill.sentence: Your laugh is loud, sure, but it's part of who you are, so stop apologizing for it and {{own it}}.
drill.hint: be proud of it instead (two words; not *embrace it*)

entries.related: *own up (to something)* — admit a mistake, without the idea of confidence; *embrace* — accept something warmly, more neutral; *take ownership of* — the business-speak version.

entries.label: slang
entries.meaning: Do whatever feels right for you; I won't judge or interfere, even if I would choose differently.
entries.usage: Slang that became popular in the 2010s, used mostly by younger adults in speech and texts as a reply to someone's plan or choice. It can be sincerely supportive or a little ironic, meaning *I wouldn't do that, but fine*; your tone decides. It can sound dismissive in a serious disagreement and is too casual for work emails.
examples: "I'm skipping the party to stay home and read." "Hey, **you do you**."
"I put ketchup on my scrambled eggs." "Weird, but **you do you**."
When I told my mom I was moving to Alaska, she just said, "Well, **you do you**, honey."

drill.sentence: "I'm dyeing my hair bright green for the summer." "Not my style, but hey, {{you do you}}."
drill.hint: follow your own taste; I won't judge (slang; not *go for it*)

entries.related: *to each their own* — similar, more neutral; *whatever floats your boat* — similar, a bit mocking; *go for it* — encourages the plan instead of just accepting it.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Said to approve of someone's decision or suggestion: that was a smart choice.
entries.usage: Very common in American speech and quick work messages, as a reply (*Good call.*) or with *on* + noun or *-ing*: *Good call on the umbrella.* *Call* here means a decision, as in sports, and *bad call* is the opposite. Fine with coworkers, even in chat with your boss, but too casual for formal writing.
examples: "I booked the earlier flight just in case." "**Good call**; the later one just got canceled."
**Good call** on bringing jackets; it's freezing up here.
Moving the launch to Monday was a **good call**, since half the team was out sick on Friday.

drill.sentence: {{Good call}} on the snacks; I had no idea the drive would take five hours.
drill.hint: you decided wisely about (two words; not *smart move*)

entries.related: *good idea* — neutral, mostly for suggestions before they happen; *smart move* — similar, about an action; *bad call* — a poor decision.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To do someone's work while they are away, or to protect them by hiding their absence or mistake, sometimes by lying.
entries.usage: Common at work and among friends and family. The work sense is neutral and fine in workplace messages (*Can you cover for me on Friday?*); the hiding sense suggests dishonesty (*Stop covering for him*). In shift work, people also say *cover someone's shift*, without *for*.
examples: Can you **cover for** me at the front desk while I run to the dentist?
My older brother always **covered for** me when I came home after curfew.
The nurse had been **covering for** a colleague's mistakes for months before anyone noticed.

drill.sentence: I'm going to be twenty minutes late; if the boss asks where I am, can you {{cover for}} me?
drill.hint: make an excuse to hide my absence (phrasal verb)

entries.related: *fill in for someone* — do someone's job for a while, no hiding; *stand in for someone* — take someone's place; *have someone's back* — be ready to support and protect them.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: A casual reply to an apology: no problem, there's no need to say sorry.
entries.usage: Very common in American speech, especially among younger adults, after small apologies such as *Sorry, am I in your way?* It is warmer and more relaxed than *no problem*. *We're good* means there is no conflict between us; neither phrase belongs in a formal email.
examples: "Oh, sorry, did I just take your seat?" "No, **you're good**, I was leaving anyway."
"Sorry I'm late!" "**You're good**; we haven't started yet."
"Sorry, am I blocking the cereal?" "Nah, **you're good**, I'm still deciding."

drill.sentence: "I'm so sorry I spilled water on your notebook!" "Oh, {{you're good}}, it's just scrap paper."
drill.hint: no need to apologize (two words; not *no worries*, *it's okay* or anything with *fine*)

entries.related: *no worries* — same use, also very common; *you're fine* — same meaning; *no problem* — neutral, also a reply to thanks.

entries.label: slang
entries.meaning: Really, seriously: as a question it checks that something is true (*For real?*); after a statement it stresses that you mean it.
entries.usage: Very common in casual American speech and texts, especially among younger speakers, who often shorten it to *fr* in messages. *For real?* sounds like *Seriously?*, and *Is he for real?* asks whether someone is serious or genuine. Too slangy for work emails, though fine with friends at work.
examples: "They're giving away free concert tickets downtown." "**For real**? Let's go."
This is the best burrito I've ever had, **for real**.
Is your coach **for real**? He wants you at practice at five a.m. on a Sunday?

drill.sentence: "I just got into my dream school!" "Wait, {{for real}}? That's amazing!"
drill.hint: are you serious? (two-word slang; not *no way*)

entries.related: *seriously* — the neutral equivalent; *no way* — shows surprise or disbelief; *legit* — slang, also means *truly*.

entries.label: slang
entries.meaning: Credit, praise and respect for something someone has done well.
entries.usage: Slang from African American and hip-hop usage, now widely used in casual speech and online. Use *props to* + person (*Props to the kitchen staff*) or *give someone props for* something; it is always plural in this sense. Warm and casual: fine in a relaxed team chat, out of place in formal writing.
entries.pattern: props to + person / give someone props (for something)
examples: **Props to** the organizers; the whole festival ran without a single delay.
I have to give my dad **props**: he finally learned to make decent coffee.
Huge **props to** everyone who stayed late to get the new website live.

drill.sentence: You ran a half marathon three months after knee surgery? Seriously, {{props}} to you.
drill.hint: credit and respect (five-letter slang; not *kudos* or *hats off*)

entries.related: *kudos* — same idea, a bit more formal and common at work; *hats off to* — same, neutral; *a shout-out* — a public mention or thanks.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A person or thing that helps you a lot at exactly the moment you need it, often by solving a small crisis.
entries.usage: Very common in everyday thanks, usually exaggerated for small favors: *You're a lifesaver!* to someone who lends you a charger. It's also used for useful objects and tools (*This app is a lifesaver*). Warm and fine in friendly work emails.
examples: You brought an extra charger? You're **a lifesaver**.
When the babysitter canceled, our neighbor stepped in; she was **a total lifesaver**.
On long flights, a good neck pillow is **a lifesaver**.

drill.sentence: Thanks for picking up my kids from school when I got stuck at work; you're {{a lifesaver}}!
drill.hint: someone who rescued me at the right moment (not *an angel*, *a saint* or *a star*)

entries.related: *a godsend* — something very helpful that arrives unexpectedly; *save the day* — solve a problem at the last moment; *a lifeline* — help that keeps a person or business going.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Far better, more advanced or more extreme than usual.
entries.usage: Casual and enthusiastic, common in talk about food, design, sports and gadgets. Use it before a noun (*next-level pizza*) or after *be* (*This is next-level*); it can also intensify something bad (*next-level rude*). In formal writing it sounds like hype, so say *exceptional* or *far more advanced* there.
examples: The brisket at that place is **next-level**; I've never had anything like it.
My neighbor's Halloween decorations are **next-level**: he built a moving dragon in his yard.
The camera on the new phone is **next-level**; you can read street signs from a block away.

drill.sentence: Have you tried the dumplings at that new spot? The sauce is {{next-level}}.
drill.hint: far beyond the usual standard (hyphenated; not *top-notch* or *world-class*)

entries.related: *on another level* — same idea, also casual; *top-notch* — excellent, a bit older; *take something to the next level* — improve it a lot, common in business talk.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: Without any doubt; used to say that something is clearly the best, worst or most of its kind.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech and reviews, usually with a superlative. It can go before the superlative (*hands down the best pizza in town*) or at the end of the sentence (*She's the best player on the team, hands down*). It sounds confident and enthusiastic; in formal writing, use *clearly* or *by far*.
examples: That was **hands down** the worst flight I've ever taken.
My grandma makes the best tamales in the family, **hands down**.
For me, the fourth season of that show is **hands down** the funniest.

drill.sentence: We've tried every coffee shop in the neighborhood, and the one on Elm Street is {{hands down}} the best.
drill.hint: without any doubt (two words; not *by far* or *no doubt*)

entries.related: *by far* — neutral, for a big difference; *easily* — similar, very common; *no contest* — casual, the comparison isn't even close.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: In the past, years ago; usually about the speaker's own younger years, often with nostalgia.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech, at the start or end of a sentence: *Back in the day, we walked to school.* It usually suggests that things were better, or at least different, then, and younger people use it jokingly for the recent past (*back in the day, like 2015*). In formal writing, use *in the past* or *years ago*.
examples: **Back in the day**, my dad could fix any car in the neighborhood.
This street was all warehouses **back in the day**; now it's coffee shops and condos.
My aunt still talks about the concerts she went to **back in the day**.

drill.sentence: My grandparents met at a dance hall that was the most popular spot in town {{back in the day}}.
drill.hint: years ago, said with nostalgia (four words; not *in the old days*)

entries.related: *in the old days* — similar, a bit more neutral; *once upon a time* — storybook style, often ironic; *these days* — the opposite, nowadays.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Traditional or old-fashioned in style or method, usually said with approval.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech about music, food, tools, people and methods: *an old-school diner*, *My dad's pretty old-school about manners.* It usually sounds warm or admiring, but it can also mean out of date. It is hyphenated before a noun and often written *old school* after a verb.
examples: We found an **old-school** diner with red booths and a jukebox.
My grandpa is **old-school**: he still writes thank-you notes by hand.
Our coach uses **old-school** training, mostly running stairs and doing push-ups.

drill.sentence: Instead of an app, my mom keeps everyone's birthdays in a paper calendar; she's very {{old-school}} that way.
drill.hint: doing things the classic way (hyphenated; not *old-fashioned*)

entries.related: *old-fashioned* — neutral, often less positive; *retro* — copying an older style on purpose; *traditional* — the standard word.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The short, intense period just before a deadline or at the end of a game, when the most important work has to happen.
entries.usage: Common at work, in school and in sports talk: *It's crunch time.* It's used without an article, usually after *it's* or in *in / at crunch time*. In the video game industry, *crunch* on its own means long periods of forced overtime, a widely criticized practice.
examples: Finals are next week, so it's **crunch time** for every student in the dorm.
Tax season is **crunch time** for accountants; my sister barely sleeps in April.
He's great all season, but he always misses free throws in **crunch time**.

drill.sentence: The science fair is tomorrow, and my son's volcano still won't erupt; it's officially {{crunch time}}.
drill.hint: the stressful final stretch before a deadline, when everything counts

entries.related: *down to the wire* — until the last possible moment; *under the gun* — under heavy time pressure; *the eleventh hour* — the last possible moment.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To stay awake all night to work, study or finish something.
entries.usage: Very common among students and also at work: *I pulled an all-nighter to finish the report.* *All-nighter* is the noun, and *pull* is the usual verb with it. It sounds casual, often a little proud or regretful.
examples: I **pulled an all-nighter** before my chemistry final and fell asleep during the exam.
We **pulled an all-nighter** packing boxes the night before the movers came.
The developers **pulled an all-nighter** to fix the bug before the app launched.

drill.sentence: I'm a zombie today; I {{pulled an all-nighter}} to finish my scholarship application.
drill.hint: worked through the whole night without sleep (not *stayed up all night*)

entries.related: *burn the midnight oil* — work late into the night; *stay up all night* — neutral; *cram* — study a lot in a short time before an exam.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To work less hard or less carefully than you should, often because the pressure is gone or nobody is watching.
entries.usage: Common at work, at school and in sports, and mildly critical: *Don't slack off just because the boss is away.* People say it about others, or about themselves with some guilt; *slack off on* + task is also common. Someone who often does this is *a slacker*.
examples: Once the manager left for vacation, half the office started **slacking off**.
I **slacked off** on my workouts over the holidays, and now my jeans are tight.
After he got into college, he **slacked off** for the rest of senior year.

drill.sentence: The coach warned us not to {{slack off}} in practice just because we'd won the first three games.
drill.hint: start working less hard than we should (not *ease up*, *let up* or *coast*)

entries.related: *goof off* — waste time instead of working; *coast* — do the minimum because things are going well; *phone it in* — do something with no real effort.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To do something with the minimum effort and no real interest, so the result is dull or careless.
entries.usage: Common in reviews of actors, musicians and athletes, and in casual talk about work: *He totally phoned it in.* It is clearly critical and suggests the person could do better but didn't care this time. *Mail it in* means the same.
examples: The lead actor clearly **phoned it in**; he barely seemed awake on screen.
After his raise was denied, he started **phoning it in** at work.
The chef must have been **phoning it in** tonight; the pasta was cold and bland.

drill.sentence: The holiday special was a disappointment; you could tell the writers were {{phoning it in}}.
drill.hint: working on autopilot, lazily (idiom with a telephone image; not *mailing it in*)

entries.related: *mail it in* — same meaning; *go through the motions* — do something without real interest; *slack off* — work less hard in general.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To produce a lot of something quickly and steadily, often without much care for quality.
entries.usage: Common in casual talk about writing, factories, music and online content: *She cranks out a novel a year.* It can be neutral or a little critical, suggesting mass production rather than craft. With a pronoun, the object goes in the middle: *crank them out*.
entries.pattern: crank out + noun / crank it out
examples: The bakery **cranks out** about two thousand bagels every morning.
That author **cranks out** three thrillers a year, and they all have the same plot.
I need to **crank out** these expense reports before Friday.

drill.sentence: Every winter my aunt {{cranks out}} dozens of scarves on her old knitting machine.
drill.hint: produces quickly and in large numbers (not *churns out*, *pumps out* or *turns out*)

mistake.wrong: These forms aren't hard; I can crank out them in an hour.
mistake.right: These forms aren't hard; I can crank them out in an hour.
mistake.why: With a pronoun object, the pronoun must go between *crank* and *out*.

entries.related: *churn out* — same, more often critical; *knock out* — finish something quickly; *turn out* — produce, neutral.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To make or prepare something quickly, especially a meal, with little time or planning.
entries.usage: Very common for food (*whip up a quick dinner*) and also used at work for slides, drafts or plans. It suggests speed and some skill, so it often sounds modest or impressed. A different sense, *whip up support or anger*, means to stir up strong feelings.
examples: Give me ten minutes and I'll **whip up** some pancakes.
Can you **whip up** a quick slide with last month's numbers before the meeting?
My roommate **whipped up** a birthday banner from old cardboard and markers.

drill.sentence: Guests are arriving in twenty minutes, but don't worry, I can {{whip up}} a salad with what's in the fridge.
drill.hint: prepare quickly (not *throw together* or *rustle up*)

entries.related: *throw together* — make quickly and roughly; *rustle up* — find or make food quickly, a bit folksy; *put together* — neutral.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A job, especially a temporary, freelance or part-time one; for musicians and comedians, a single paid performance.
entries.usage: Very common in casual talk about work: *a side gig*, *a teaching gig*, *land a gig*. People also call a regular job *a gig* in casual speech (*How's the new gig?*), and *the gig economy* is the standard news term for short, app-based jobs.
examples: She's got a weekend **gig** teaching swim lessons to help pay off her student loans.
How's the new **gig**? Do you like your coworkers?
His band played their first paid **gig** at a bar in Austin last night.

drill.sentence: Between his day job and a side {{gig}} DJing parties on weekends, he barely sleeps.
drill.hint: short-term paid work (not *hustle* or *job*)

entries.related: *side hustle* — extra work for money besides a main job; *freelance work* — neutral; *a temp job* — short-term work, often through an agency.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A quick summary of the main points or facts about something.
entries.usage: Common at work and in everyday talk: *Can you give me a quick rundown?* Usually *give someone a rundown of / on* something, or *get the rundown*; it's casual but fine in meetings and friendly work messages. Don't confuse it with the adjective *run-down* (in poor condition, or tired).
entries.pattern: give someone a (quick) rundown of / on something
examples: Before the meeting, Lisa gave me a quick **rundown** of what the client wants.
Can you give me **the rundown** on the new neighbors? Are they nice?
The tour guide gave us a five-minute **rundown** on the history of the castle.

drill.sentence: I missed the first half of the game; can you give me a quick {{rundown}} of what happened?
drill.hint: short version of the main events (not *recap* or *summary*)

entries.related: *a recap* — a summary of what already happened; *the gist* — the main idea; *a briefing* — formal information before an event.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: A little; slightly. Used before an adjective or adverb (*a tad expensive*) or with *more* and *less* (*a tad more salt*).
entries.usage: Casual and a bit playful, often used to soften a criticism politely: *The soup is a tad salty.* Because it understates, it is often ironic about something much bigger (*a tad late* for a three-hour delay). Fine in friendly work emails.
examples: The steak was great, but the sauce was **a tad** too sweet for me.
Could you turn the music down **a tad**? The baby's asleep.
Your brother's speech ran **a tad** long; we were there until midnight.

drill.sentence: I love the dress, but it's {{a tad}} too tight around the shoulders.
drill.hint: a small amount (*a* + a three-letter word; not *a bit*)

entries.related: *a bit* — the most common neutral choice; *a touch* — similar, a little more refined; *slightly* — neutral, good in writing.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A thousand dollars (in Britain, a thousand pounds); *five grand* means $5,000.
entries.usage: Common in casual talk about prices, salaries and bets: *It cost me two grand.* After a number the plural is also *grand* (*ten grand*, not *ten grands*). Informal writing often uses *K* instead (*a $60K salary*), but neither belongs in formal documents.
examples: The repair on my car came to almost three **grand**.
She paid **a grand** for the couch, and the cat ruined it in a week.
The new job pays about ten **grand** more a year, plus better health insurance.

drill.sentence: Our family trip to Disney World ended up costing about six {{grand}}, including flights.
drill.hint: informal word for thousands of dollars (not *thousand* or *K*)

mistake.wrong: The new roof cost us twelve grands.
mistake.right: The new roof cost us twelve grand.
mistake.why: *Grand* takes no plural *-s* after a number.

entries.related: *a buck* — a dollar; *K* — informal written form (*50K*); *a thousand bucks* — the same amount, also casual.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: Of sales, prices, ratings or performance: to fail badly or fall sharply.
entries.usage: Common in business news and casual talk: *The stock tanked after the earnings report.* It's usually used without an object; in sports, *tank a game* or *tank the season* means to lose on purpose. Fine in spoken business talk, but too casual for formal reports, where *fall sharply* or *plummet* fit.
examples: Home prices in our area **tanked** when the factory closed.
My grades **tanked** the semester I worked two jobs.
The movie **tanked** at the box office, earning back less than half its budget.

drill.sentence: Their ratings {{tanked}} after the host left, and the network canceled the show.
drill.hint: describes a sudden, steep fall (informal; not *crashed* or *sank*)

entries.related: *plummet* — fall very fast, neutral; *crater* — fall sharply, informal; *bomb* — fail badly, used for tests and shows.

entries.label: slang
entries.meaning: To do something extremely well, such as a performance, a game, an exam or a job.
entries.usage: Enthusiastic slang, common in speech, texts, sports and startup culture: *You crushed it!* is a very common compliment after a presentation or a game. Use the past tense to praise (*She crushed it*) and the future to encourage (*You're going to crush it*). Fine with coworkers in speech or chat, too casual for formal writing.
examples: You **crushed it** at the talent show; my kids haven't stopped humming your song.
"How did the interview go?" "Honestly, I think I **crushed it**."
The rookie **crushed it** in her first game, scoring twenty-eight points.

drill.sentence: Our softball team {{crushed it}} last night, with twelve runs in the first three innings.
drill.hint: did brilliantly (slang; not *killed it*, *nailed it* or *smashed it*)

entries.related: *kill it* — same meaning; *nail it* — do exactly right; *ace* — do very well on a test or interview.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Something that is certain to succeed, or a case or decision so clear that there is no real doubt.
entries.usage: From basketball, where a slam dunk is a shot pushed straight down through the hoop that almost never misses. Common in business, sports and legal talk (*The case looked like a slam dunk*), and often used with *no* to warn that success isn't guaranteed: *It's no slam dunk.* It sounds confident and casual.
examples: With three witnesses and a video, the prosecutors thought the case was **a slam dunk**.
The new restaurant looked like **a slam dunk**, but it closed within a year.
Getting a permit for a small deck should be **a slam dunk**; my neighbor got one in a week.

drill.sentence: She's the most qualified candidate by far, so her promotion is {{a slam dunk}}.
drill.hint: certain to succeed (basketball image; not *a sure thing* or *a lock*)

entries.related: *a sure thing* — certain to happen; *a lock* — US sports slang for a certain winner; *a no-brainer* — an obvious decision.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To commit completely to something, putting all your money, time or effort into it and accepting the risk.
entries.usage: From poker, where *going all in* means betting all your chips. Common in business, sports and personal decisions; use *go all in on* + noun, or *be all in* (= be fully committed). It suggests boldness and can sound admiring or warn of recklessness, depending on the result.
examples: After ten years in banking, he **went all in** on his dream of opening a brewery.
The city is **going all in** on electric buses, replacing its whole fleet by 2030.
If we're signing up for this marathon, let's **go all in** and train properly.

drill.sentence: Instead of testing the idea first, they {{went all in}} and spent their entire savings on a food truck.
drill.hint: committed everything at once (poker image; not the idiom ending in *for broke*)

entries.related: *go for broke* — risk everything for a big success; *bet the farm* — risk everything you own; *dip a toe in* — the opposite, try something carefully.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To try something, often for the first time, to see whether it works or whether you like it.
entries.usage: Very common in everyday speech and fine at work: *Why not give it a shot?* Put *it* or a noun between *give* and *a shot* (*give yoga a shot*). *Give it a try* means the same, *give it a go* sounds a little more British, and *give it your best shot* means try as hard as you can.
examples: I'd never tried rock climbing, but my friends talked me into **giving it a shot**.
The new scheduling system looks confusing, but let's **give it a shot** for a week.
My doctor suggested I **give physical therapy a shot** before thinking about surgery.

drill.sentence: I've never cooked Thai food before, but I found an easy recipe, so I'm going to {{give it a shot}}.
drill.hint: attempt it and see how it goes (four words; not ending in *a try*, *a go* or *a whirl*)

entries.related: *give it a try* — same, neutral; *take a stab at something* — try something you're not sure you can do; *a long shot* — something unlikely to succeed.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A situation where two outcomes or choices are equally likely or equally good, so you can't predict or decide.
entries.usage: Common in sports, elections and everyday choices: *It's a toss-up between the two teams.* Usually *it's a toss-up* or *a toss-up between A and B*; the image is a coin toss. Casual in tone, but also used in news writing.
entries.pattern: it's a toss-up (between A and B / whether …)
examples: Pizza or tacos tonight? Honestly, it's **a toss-up**.
With both teams missing their best players, Sunday's game is **a toss-up**.
The forecast says it's **a toss-up** whether the parade gets rained out.

drill.sentence: Both apartments are great, so choosing between them is really {{a toss-up}}.
drill.hint: a choice that could go either way (not *a coin flip* or *fifty-fifty*)

entries.related: *a coin flip* — same idea; *fifty-fifty* — equal chances; *anyone's guess* — impossible to know.

entries.label: adjective phrase
entries.meaning: Sometimes good and sometimes bad, so you can't rely on the quality or the result.
entries.usage: Common in reviews and casual talk about restaurants, services and methods: *The service there is hit or miss.* It usually follows *be*; before a noun it's often hyphenated (*a hit-or-miss approach*). It's a mild criticism of inconsistency; British speakers also say *hit-and-miss*.
examples: The food at that diner is **hit or miss**: the burgers are great, but the fries are often cold.
Cell service out at the lake house is **hit or miss**, so download your maps before you go.
Finding a good babysitter through online ads is pretty **hit or miss**.

drill.sentence: My neighbor's tomatoes are {{hit or miss}}: some summers they're amazing, and some summers the squirrels get them all.
drill.hint: good one year, bad the next (three-word phrase)

entries.related: *hit-and-miss* — same, more common in British English; *spotty* — uneven in quality, casual; *a mixed bag* — some good parts, some bad.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A small, temporary problem or delay that interrupts something but doesn't cause serious harm.
entries.usage: Common at work and in the news, often to make a problem sound minor: *a slight hiccup with the booking*. Typical with *minor*, *small* or *slight*. Because it downplays problems, it can sound evasive when a company uses it for something serious.
examples: There was **a slight hiccup** with our hotel booking, but they found us another room.
Apart from **a few hiccups** with the sound system, the wedding went perfectly.
The airline called the three-hour check-in outage **a minor hiccup**.

drill.sentence: We had a small {{hiccup}} when the moving truck showed up late, but everything was unpacked by dinner.
drill.hint: short, minor interruption (not *snag*, *glitch*, *delay* or *problem*)

entries.related: *a snag* — an unexpected problem, similar; *a glitch* — a small technical fault; *a setback* — something that delays progress, more serious.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A surprising result that happens by chance, not because of skill or a real pattern.
entries.usage: Common in sports, school and everyday talk, often to dismiss someone's success: *Their win was a fluke.* *No fluke* praises a success as earned (*Her second win proved it was no fluke*), and *a total fluke* describes a strange coincidence. In science, a result that might be *a fluke* is one that may not repeat.
examples: Everyone said our first win was **a fluke**, so beating them again felt amazing.
It was **a total fluke** that I ran into my old roommate at an airport in Tokyo.
Let's rerun the experiment to make sure the result wasn't **a fluke**.

drill.sentence: She aced the first test, and when she aced the second one too, everyone realized it wasn't {{a fluke}}.
drill.hint: a result of chance alone, not skill (not *luck*, *a one-off* or *a coincidence*)

entries.related: *beginner's luck* — success by chance when you're new; *a coincidence* — two things happening together by chance; *a one-off* — something that happens only once.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To get something you want, often by luck or clever effort, such as tickets, a deal or a good table.
entries.usage: Casual American speech, often in excited stories: *We scored front-row seats!* It takes a direct object (*score a deal*, *score free tickets*), and *Score!* alone is a happy reaction to getting something. Too casual for formal writing.
examples: My sister **scored** two free tickets to the playoff game from a coworker.
We **scored** a great parking spot right in front of the restaurant.
I **scored** this vintage lamp at a thrift store for eight bucks.

drill.sentence: I can't believe we {{scored}} a table at that place without a reservation on a Friday night!
drill.hint: obtained, with luck (one word; not *snagged*, *grabbed* or *got*)

entries.related: *snag* — get something quickly before others do; *land* — get something you worked for (*land a job*); *luck out* — be lucky in general.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To get or grab something quickly or by luck, often before someone else does.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech and ads: *Snag a deal before it's gone.* It's used for small, everyday things (*snag a table*, *snag a coffee*, *snag me one too*). As a noun, *a snag* means a small problem (*We hit a snag*), a different sense.
examples: Get there early if you want to **snag** a seat near the stage.
I **snagged** the last two croissants at the bakery this morning.
Can you **snag** me a coffee on your way in?

drill.sentence: Concert tickets go on sale at ten, so set an alarm if you want to {{snag}} good seats.
drill.hint: obtain quickly, before others do (not *grab*, *get*, *nab* or *score*)

entries.related: *grab* — take or get quickly, very common; *score* — get something good, often by luck; *nab* — get or catch quickly, similar.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Rather expensive; costing more than you expected or want to pay.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech and reviews: *The food is great but pricey.* It's softer than *expensive* and often comes with *a bit*, *a little* or *kind of*. The other forms are *pricier* and *priciest*.
examples: That sushi place is amazing, but it's a little **pricey** for a weeknight.
Flights to Hawaii get really **pricey** around the holidays.
We looked at a few strollers, and the **pricier** ones weren't much better.

drill.sentence: The hotel was nice but a bit {{pricey}}, so next time we'll look for something cheaper.
drill.hint: costing more than we liked (informal adjective; not *expensive* or *steep*)

entries.related: *expensive* — neutral; *steep* — of a price, too high (*a steep price*); *spendy* — informal, regional American.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Something that costs far more than it is worth, so you feel cheated.
entries.usage: Common in casual complaints about prices, often as an exclamation: *Twelve dollars for a beer, what a rip-off!* The verb is *rip someone off* (*They ripped us off*), and *feel ripped off* is very common. The noun is written *rip-off* or *ripoff*.
examples: Eight dollars for a bottle of water at the stadium is **a total rip-off**.
The premium cable package was **a rip-off**; we only watched three channels.
What **a rip-off**! The family-size bag of chips is half air.

drill.sentence: They charged us forty dollars for parking at the concert; what {{a rip-off}}!
drill.hint: an overpriced deal that leaves you feeling cheated (not *a scam*)

entries.related: *a scam* — a dishonest trick to take money; *overpriced* — the neutral adjective; *a steal* — the opposite, a great bargain.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Something you buy for much less than it is really worth; an excellent bargain.
entries.usage: Common in shopping talk and real estate ads: *At $20, it's a steal.* Usually after *be* (*It was a steal*), often with *at that price* or *for* + price. It's the opposite of *a rip-off*.
examples: I got this leather jacket for thirty bucks at a yard sale; it was **a steal**.
At that price, the house is **a steal**, even with the old roof.
Fifty dollars for a whole season of swimming lessons? That's **a steal**.

drill.sentence: Front-row seats for twenty dollars? That's {{a steal}}; buy them before they're gone.
drill.hint: so cheap it's almost like taking it for free (not *a deal* or *a bargain*)

entries.related: *a bargain* — neutral; *a good deal* — neutral, very common; *a rip-off* — the opposite.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To pay a lot of money for something, usually unwillingly or more than you think is fair.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech and journalism: *We had to shell out $800 for a new fridge.* Use *shell out* + amount (*for* something) or *shell out for* something. It always suggests that the cost hurts.
examples: We had to **shell out** six hundred dollars to fix the dishwasher.
Fans are **shelling out** hundreds for tickets on resale sites.
I'm not **shelling out** for a new phone when mine still works fine.

drill.sentence: If you lose your apartment key, you'll have to {{shell out}} a hundred bucks for a new lock.
drill.hint: hand over money you'd rather keep (not *fork out*, *cough up* or *pay*)

entries.related: *fork over / fork out* — same idea; *cough up* — pay unwillingly, often money you owe; *splurge* — spend a lot happily, as a treat.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To spend more money than usual on something you enjoy, as a special treat.
entries.usage: Common in everyday talk and lifestyle writing: *We splurged on a nice hotel.* Use *splurge on* + thing; it's also a noun (*a splurge*). It sounds positive or self-forgiving, unlike *waste money*.
examples: For our anniversary, we **splurged on** a fancy dinner downtown.
These boots were **a splurge**, but I wear them every day.
Let's **splurge** and get the room with the ocean view.

drill.sentence: We usually stay in cheap motels, but for our honeymoon we decided to {{splurge}} on a resort in Maui.
drill.hint: spend generously as a treat (not *go all out*)

entries.related: *treat yourself* — enjoy something special; *go all out* — make a big effort or spend a lot; *shell out* — pay a lot unwillingly.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To give a share of money or help so that a group can pay for or do something together.
entries.usage: Very common at work, at home and among friends: *Everyone chipped in for her birthday present.* Use *chip in for* a thing, *chip in* + amount, or *chip in to* + verb. It sounds friendly and cooperative.
examples: My brothers and I **chipped in** to buy our parents a new TV for their anniversary.
If we each **chip in** twenty bucks, we can rent a cabin for the weekend.
The whole neighborhood **chipped in** to help the family after the fire.

drill.sentence: The pizza came to sixty dollars, so the four of us {{chipped in}} fifteen each.
drill.hint: each gave a share of the cost (phrasal verb; not *pitched in*, *put in* or *paid*)

entries.related: *pitch in* — help with work, or contribute money; *split the bill* — share the cost equally; *pool money* — put money together for a shared purchase.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A dollar; *five bucks* means $5.
entries.usage: Extremely common in casual American speech about prices and money: *It's only ten bucks.* It also appears in fixed phrases like *make a quick buck* (earn money easily, often in a shady way) and *pass the buck* (shift responsibility to someone else). Too casual for formal writing.
examples: Can you lend me five **bucks** for the parking meter?
The tacos are only two **bucks** each on Tuesdays.
Some landlords just want to make **a quick buck** off students.

drill.sentence: The movie theater charges eight {{bucks}} for a small popcorn, which is crazy.
drill.hint: informal word for dollars (not *dollars*)

entries.related: *a grand* — a thousand dollars; *a dime* — ten cents; *a quarter* — twenty-five cents.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To earn a lot of money, often easily or quickly.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech and journalism, often with an envious or critical tone: *Ticket resellers are raking in millions.* It's often in the progressive, and *rake it in* means to make a lot of money. The object is money: *cash*, *profits*, *millions*.
entries.pattern: rake in + money / rake it in
examples: The ice cream truck **rakes in** a fortune on hot summer weekends.
The airlines **raked in** record profits during the holiday season.
My cousin sells custom sneakers online, and he's **raking it in**.

drill.sentence: With three food trucks at every festival, she's {{raking in}} more than she ever made as a lawyer.
drill.hint: money is pouring in for her (not *bringing in*, *pulling in* or *making*)

entries.related: *rolling in it* — very rich; *make a killing* — make a lot of money quickly; *bring in* — earn, neutral.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Excessive publicity and excitement about something, often more than it deserves.
entries.usage: Very common about movies, products, restaurants and new technology. Typical patterns are *live up to the hype*, *believe the hype* and *all the hype around / about* something. *Hype* is also a verb (*hype something up*), and in slang *hyped* means excited.
entries.pattern: live up to the hype / all the hype around something
examples: After all **the hype**, the new burger place was just okay.
The sequel totally lived up to **the hype**; I'd see it again tomorrow.
Don't buy into **the hype**; that new air fryer is just a small oven with a fan.

drill.sentence: Everyone raved about the show, but honestly, it didn't live up to {{the hype}}.
drill.hint: all the excited publicity around it (not *expectations*)

entries.related: *buzz* — excited talk about something new, more neutral; *overhyped* — praised more than it deserves; *hyped* — slang for excited.

entries.label: slang
entries.meaning: To stop supporting a public figure or brand, often as part of a wide online reaction, after they have said or done something seen as offensive.
entries.usage: Slang from social media since the late 2010s, often in the passive (*He got canceled*) and in the noun *cancel culture*. People use it seriously, critically or as a joke among friends (*You're canceled* for a tiny offense). The topic is sensitive: some see canceling as accountability and others as public shaming, so be careful with it in serious discussion.
examples: The comedian got **canceled** after some of his old jokes resurfaced online.
"You put pineapple on pizza? Sorry, you're **canceled**."
The brand was briefly **canceled** online over a tone-deaf ad, but its sales barely changed.

drill.sentence: The singer was {{canceled}} online after a video of him yelling at a waiter went viral.
drill.hint: publicly dropped by fans as punishment (slang; not *dragged* or *boycotted*)

entries.related: *cancel culture* — the wider practice, usually said critically; *call someone out* — publicly criticize someone for a wrong; *boycott* — refuse to buy or support, neutral.

entries.label: slang
entries.meaning: Originally, alert to social injustice, especially racism; now often used by critics as an insult for views they see as too progressive.
entries.usage: It comes from African American English, where *stay woke* meant stay aware of injustice. Since the late 2010s it has been used more and more by critics, often mockingly, so few people now describe themselves as *woke* without irony. It is politically loaded: avoid it in neutral or professional writing unless you are discussing the word itself.
examples: "Stay **woke**" began in African American speech as a reminder to stay alert to injustice.
Some critics praised the film, while others dismissed it as **woke**.
My brother thinks he's so **woke** now that he brings his own bags to the grocery store.

drill.sentence: These days, the word {{woke}} is more often used as a jab by critics than as praise.
drill.hint: slang that once meant alert to social injustice

entries.related: *politically correct (PC)* — an older term used in similar ways; *socially conscious* — a neutral description; *woke* — also the normal past tense of *wake* (*I woke up at six*).

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To manipulate someone into doubting their own memory, perception or judgment, for example by insisting that things they remember never happened.
entries.usage: The term comes from the play and film *Gaslight*, in which a husband tries to make his wife believe she is losing her mind. It began as a term for serious psychological abuse but is now very common in casual speech, sometimes loosely or jokingly for any denial. It's a serious accusation, so use it with care; the past tense is *gaslit* or *gaslighted*.
examples: Her ex used to **gaslight** her, insisting that fights she clearly remembered had never happened.
My manager keeps **gaslighting** the team, denying he ever set the deadline he gave us in writing.
"You **gaslit** me; you said the party was casual!" she joked, standing there in a hoodie.

drill.sentence: My brother swears he never borrowed my headphones, even though I saw him wearing them; he's totally {{gaslighting}} me.
drill.hint: trying to make me doubt what I saw (not *lying to*)

entries.related: *manipulate* — control someone unfairly, more general; *mess with someone's head* — confuse someone on purpose, casual; *deny* — say something isn't true, neutral.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: An attempt to make someone feel guilty so that they will do what you want.
entries.usage: Common in casual talk about family and relationships: *My mom gave me a guilt trip for not calling.* Typical patterns are *give someone a guilt trip* and *lay a guilt trip on someone*, and the verb is *guilt-trip someone (into something)*. It is critical: people use it for others' behavior, rarely their own.
entries.pattern: give someone / lay a guilt trip on someone; guilt-trip someone into something
examples: Every time I skip Sunday dinner, my mom gives me **a guilt trip** about how rarely she sees me.
Don't **guilt-trip** me into working this weekend; I already said no.
The charity's ad felt like **a guilt trip**, with sad music and shivering puppies.

drill.sentence: I said I couldn't help him move, and he laid {{a guilt trip}} on me about all the times he'd helped me.
drill.hint: an effort to make me feel bad so I'd change my mind

entries.related: *emotional blackmail* — a stronger, more serious term; *make someone feel bad* — neutral; *pressure someone* — push someone to do something, more general.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To make someone laugh a lot.
entries.usage: Very common and friendly in casual speech, often as a compliment about someone's humor: *You crack me up.* The object goes between *crack* and *up* (*cracks me up*, *cracked everyone up*). Without an object, *crack up* means to start laughing hard (*We all cracked up*).
examples: My grandpa's stories about his army days always **crack** us **up**.
My coworker **cracked** the whole room **up** with one deadpan comment about the printer.
The whole class **cracked up** when the teacher's slides showed a photo of her cat by mistake.

drill.sentence: My little niece does a perfect impression of her dad; it {{cracks me up}} every time.
drill.hint: makes me burst out laughing (phrasal verb with *me* in the middle; not *kills me*)

entries.related: *make someone laugh* — neutral; *kill someone* — slang, as in *You're killing me*; *have someone in stitches* — make someone laugh uncontrollably.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To make someone feel uneasy, uncomfortable or a little scared, often because something seems strange or wrong.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech: *That doll creeps me out.* The object goes in the middle, and the past tense is *creeped*, not *crept* (*It totally creeped me out*); *creeped out* also works as an adjective. The related adjective is *creepy*.
examples: Abandoned malls really **creep me out**, especially at night.
The way he kept staring at us from across the bar totally **creeped** my friend **out**.
Smart speakers that start talking on their own **creep** a lot of people **out**.

drill.sentence: I don't like that old house at the end of our street; the boarded-up windows really {{creep me out}}.
drill.hint: make me uneasy and a little scared (phrasal verb; not *freak me out*)

mistake.wrong: That movie really crept me out.
mistake.right: That movie really creeped me out.
mistake.why: In this phrasal verb the past tense is *creeped*; *crept* is the past of *creep* meaning to move slowly and quietly.

entries.related: *freak someone out* — upset or scare someone more strongly; *give someone the creeps* — same meaning; *unsettle* — neutral, a bit formal.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To amaze or impress someone completely, often by showing them something they had never imagined.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech about facts, performances, food and technology: *This will blow your mind.* Related forms are the adjective *mind-blowing* and the text reaction *mind blown*. It's enthusiastic, and overused in clickbait (*facts that will blow your mind*).
examples: The first time I saw the northern lights, it completely **blew my mind**.
Wait, octopuses have three hearts? That **blows my mind**.
Showing my kids how a record player works totally **blew their minds**.

drill.sentence: When I learned that bananas are technically berries but strawberries aren't, it {{blew my mind}}.
drill.hint: left me completely astonished, as if my head exploded (not *floored me* or *amazed me*)

entries.related: *blow someone away* — impress someone greatly; *floor someone* — surprise someone so much they can't react; *mind-boggling* — too strange or big to understand.
